NGL
EN-jee-EL (or spoken in full)
abbreviation (Gen-Z slang)
Text abbreviation of not gonna lie ("not going to lie"), a spoken American hedge that grew common in the 2000s as a softener before an admission or an opinion ("not gonna lie, I cried"). The initialism ngl spread on Twitter and Tumblr in the early 2010s and became a TikTok and group-chat staple c. 2018–2020.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang ngl introduces a mild confession or an honest opinion: "ngl that movie was mid," "ngl I’m kind of nervous." It works like a raised hand: what follows is unvarnished. Most of the time it is harmless, and sometimes it opens real candour between friends. The Christian observation: the phrase carries a quiet assumption — that without the label, lying would be on the table. For a believer there should be no gear change between ordinary speech and honest speech. "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another" (Eph 4:25). "Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds" (Col 3:9). Paul defended his own word on exactly this ground: "as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay" (2Co 1:18). The man who may dwell on God’s holy hill "speaketh the truth in his heart" (Psa 15:2) — not only in the sentences flagged as honest. Solomon makes no exception for the small social lie: "Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight" (Pro 12:22). And beneath all of it stands Christ, who said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (Joh 14:6); His people tell the truth because they belong to the Truth. A father tells his daughter: use the phrase if you like, but live so that it is redundant — so that everyone who knows you assumes you are not lying, because you never do.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z text-speak (spoken 2000s; ngl online 2010s–present) for "not gonna lie," a softener before a confession or opinion — harmless in use, but a reminder that a Christian’s every word should already be true.

expand to see more

NGL, abbr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2010–present; spoken form earlier) "Not gonna lie"; introduces a frank opinion or small confession. "Ngl I kind of liked the old version better."

Placed at the start or end of a sentence: "that test was hard ngl." Spoken in full as "not gonna lie" or "I’m not gonna lie." Close kin to tbh.

Older relatives a grandparent will know: "to tell you the truth," "honestly," "I’ll be frank" — the same hedge in older dress.

Webster (1828), root word lie: “LIE, noun 1. A criminal falsehood; a falsehood uttered for the purpose of deception; an intentional violation of truth. Fiction, or a false statement or representation, not intended to deceive, mislead or injure, as in fables, parables and the like, is not a lie It is willful deceit that makes a lie A man may act a lie as by pointing his …”

Decode for parents: usually a harmless softener; listen for whether your child treats honesty as a special occasion.

Key Scripture

Eph 4:25 — "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another."

Col 3:9 — "Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds;"

2Co 1:18 — "But as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay."

Psa 15:2 — "He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart."

Pro 12:22 — "Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight."

Modern Corruption

NGL is a harmless softener on its face, but it quietly sorts speech into flagged-honest and unflagged, when Scripture asks for one kind only.

expand to see more

Most uses of ngl are innocent; a teen admitting he cried at a film is not sinning by prefacing it. The trouble is the habit of mind the phrase can grow. If honesty needs announcing, then the default must be something less — the polite fib, the exaggeration, the story shaded to look better. A generation raised online has learned that every post is curated, and ngl becomes the small label on the rare unfiltered sentence. That is backwards. The believer has "put off the old man with his deeds" (Col 3:9), and lying is one of the garments that came off with him.

Paul was accused of being a man whose word shifted — yes today, no tomorrow — and his defence was theological: "as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay" (2Co 1:18). The faithfulness of God is the ground of a Christian’s plain speech. We do not tell the truth because a phrase warns that we are about to; we tell it because we are "members one of another" (Eph 4:25) and belong to the God who cannot lie. Let your children say ngl if they like; teach them that for a Christian it should always be true already.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English leogan (to lie) → spoken hedge "not gonna lie" (2000s) → ngl on Twitter and Tumblr (early 2010s) → TikTok and texting staple.

expand to see more

Old English leogan — to tell a falsehood

Older hedges: "to tell the truth," "honestly," "frankly"

2000s American speech: "not gonna lie" before a confession or opinion

Early 2010s: initialism ngl on Twitter and Tumblr

c. 2018–present: TikTok captions and group chats
